title: Automated Maintenance Coordinator for Dedicated Fleets
creator: Connor Liu
description:
Problem statement:
Customers on Dedicated capacity need predictable throughput guarantees and low-latency slices even while we perform routine node lifecycle operations (draining, upgrades, hardware retirement). Today: maintenance is manual or semi-automated and can cause temporary throughput degradation, cache misses, or uneven traffic routing. We need an automated coordinator service that schedules maintenance windows, sequences node drains/upgrades, coordinates with autoscaling policies and throughput guards, and provides observability and rollback controls.

Scope & non-goals:
- In scope: automated maintenance windows, graceful cordon+drain sequences, integration with autoscaler to avoid capacity cliffs, preserving KV/prefix caches where possible, upgrade sequencing across AZs, maintenance API and console controls, runbook and on-call playbook.
- Out of scope: full hardware reprovisioning workflows, auto-replacement of failed GPUs (separate reliability task), deep integration with third-party provisioning systems beyond basic hooks.

Why this matters:
- Prevents customer-visible throughput drops during maintenance by coordinating draining with autoscaling and temporary capacity reservations.
- Reduces manual toil for SREs and capacity owners.
- Enables safe rolling upgrades and predictable maintenance SLAs for Dedicated customers.

High-level approach:
1) Maintenance Coordinator service: centralized scheduler that owns maintenance windows for a fleet and exposes REST/SDK controls.
2) Draining orchestrator: performs cordon -> gradual drain (respecting in-flight request timeout and KV cache transfer policy) -> post-drain health check.
3) Autoscaler integration: coordinator requests temporary burst capacity or throttles drain rate based on live throughput SLOs and configured throughput guarantees per customer.
4) Upgrade sequencing: orchestrate upgrades by zone/partition with safe concurrency limits and canary nodes.
5) Observability & controls: console UI to schedule windows, abort/pause, view per-node progress, and audit log entries for each step.

Key trade-offs considered:
- Fast drain vs cache warmness: faster drains free nodes quicker but cause more cache misses and higher token cost on remaining nodes. We'll support drain-rate tuning and an option to transfer KV cache snapshots for critical workloads.
- Reservation of burst capacity vs cost: reserving buffer capacity during maintenance increases cost; default policy will attempt autoscaler bursting first, fall back to delaying maintenance if constraints fail.
- Coordinator single-point-of-control vs distributed agents: start centralized for visibility and simplicity, design protocol so agents can be made more distributed later.

Design notes and interfaces:
- New API endpoints: POST /maintenance/windows, GET /maintenance/windows/{id}, POST /maintenance/windows/{id}/actions (start/pause/abort).
- Node agent extension: drain phases reported via /agent/v1/drain-status; agent accepts cordon/drain/rollback commands.
- Autoscaler hook: coordinator posts planned drain plan (list of nodes with expected start times and capacity delta) to /autoscaler/v1/plans; autoscaler responds with approval and suggested throttle.
- Console: maintenance calendar and per-window live timeline.

Acceptance criteria (see list below) and testing:
- Unit and integration tests for coordinator, agent drain state machine, and autoscaler handshake.
- E2E staging run that triggers a simulated maintenance window on a fleet of 50 nodes without violating per-route throughput SLOs.
- Instrumentation: events, per-node metrics (drain_start, drain_complete, evicted_sessions), and alert when drain fails or takes >2x expected time.

Artifacts and links:
- Design doc: https://confluence.company/internal/dedicated/automated-maintenance-coordinator (placeholder link)
- Staging dashboard: https://grafana.company/d/maintenance/staging (placeholder link)
- Initial PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/432 (agent changes), https://github.com/redwood-inference/control-plane/pull/198 (coordinator)
acceptance_criteria: Coordinator can schedule a maintenance window and persist it to the control plane
Coordinator sends a drain plan to agents and receives stepwise progress updates
Autoscaler accepts drain plans and recommends throttle/temporary capacity; coordinator honours recommendations
Rolling upgrades run by zone with <10% concurrent node drains in a zone by default
Metrics emitted for drain latency, evicted sessions, and post-drain error spike; alerts configured
Console shows live progress and allows abort/pause with audit log entries
Staging E2E run demonstrates no route falls below configured throughput guarantee during maintenance
rollout_plan: Phase 1: Merge coordinator and agent changes behind feature flags; run in isolated staging fleet (Q1 end)
Phase 2: Run multiple staged maintenance windows on non-production Dedicated fleets and collect metrics (2 weeks)
Phase 3: Beta with 3 pilot customers on dedicated-qa for low-risk windows; collect feedback and refine throttle heuristics (1 month)
Phase 4: GA behind opt-in on dedicated tenants then on-by-default with documentation and cost guidance
risks: Autoscaler rejection of drain plans leading to delayed maintenance; mitigated by backoff and human alerting
Large tenant with strict throughput SLAs may still experience degradation; mitigation: pre-reserved burst capacity option and tenant opt-out
Bug in agent drain state machine could evict requests prematurely; mitigation: thorough staging tests and canary nodes
